answers.answer: In case A, the 09:02 request can use the original 09:00 copy because its TTL has not expired, but that copy is stale after the source changed at 09:01. The original entry expires at 09:05, so the 09:06 request cannot use it; the API gets a cache miss, fetches the source, stores a copy, and returns it. In separate case B, removal at 09:03 is eviction to make room, even though the TTL would last until 09:05. The 09:04 request therefore misses and the API must fetch the source and fill the cache. Neither eviction nor expiration fetches a replacement itself: this cache-aside API does the work on a later miss. Five minutes of TTL promises a limit on the lifetime of that entry, not five minutes of fresh data or a scheduled refresh. The original data can become stale during the TTL, and an entry can disappear earlier through eviction. No teaching needed to answer this scenario is missing.

evidence.quote: Sets how long an entry may remain before it expires. A 60-second TTL does not refresh the product every minute; a later miss must load it again.
Removes entries to make room. A least-recently-used policy favors removing entries that have not been read recently.
A product can be evicted before its TTL ends. Some configurations reject new entries when full instead of evicting existing ones.
TTL limits an entry's lifetime, not the age of the source data used to fill it.
The API checks and fills the cache explicitly. The cache does not fetch the product from the database on its own.
The entry is absent. The API reads the database, stores a copy in the cache, and returns the details.
A hit can still return an old price. Finding a value does not prove it matches the database.
